Recently, while driving from Washington D.C. to New England with my own family, I tried explaining all this to my children and got the idea that we should stop for the night at an old-fashioned family-run establishment. Everyone thought **this** was an extremely stupid idea, but I insisted that it would be a great experience.

Well, we looked everywhere. We passed scores of motels, but they were all franchised (授权) to national chains. Eventually, after perhaps 90 minutes of fruitless hunting, I pulled off the interstate (州际公路) for the seventh or eighth time and—lo!—there shining out of the darkness was the Sleepy Hollow Motel, a perfect 1950s sort of place.
"There's a Comfort Inn across the street," one of my children pointed out.
"We don't want a Comfort Inn, Jimmy," I explained, temporarily forgetting in my excitement that I don't have a child named Jimmy. "We want a real motel."

My wife, being English, insisted on having a look at the room. It was awful, of course. The furnishings (陈设) were old and bare. The room was so cold you could see your breath. There was a shower curtain, but it hung by just three rings.
"We'll be across the road at the Comfort Inn," my wife said.
In disbelief, I watched them troop out.
"You'll stay, won't you, Jimmy?" I said, but even he left without a backward glance.

I stood there for about 15 seconds, then switched off the light, returned the key, and went across to the Comfort Inn. It was characterless and just like every other Comfort Inn I had ever stayed in. But it was clean, the TV worked, and, it must be said, the shower curtain was very nice.

Imagine winning the lottery (彩票) and never having to worry about money again. Would you travel the world, drive a sports car and live in a fancy house? Catherine Herdman's dream came true in January 2011 when she won nearly £1.2 million. But her life has remained surprisingly unluxurious. Ten years ago, the hairdresser was a single parent who had to watch her pennies and couldn't always afford to turn the heating on.

As a teenager, she trained as a hairdresser for a living. After the National Lottery was launched in 1994, she would get a ticket for herself. She continued using the same numbers, convinced they would one day come up. Later she started her own salon and had to be careful when she put the heading on. But she had enough to get by. Life remained so until one day after she turned 40 when she won nearly £1.2 million. While most lottery winners take a luxury holiday or spend money like water, Catherine—incredibly—didn't want the rest of her life to change.

Five months after her big win, Catherine began dating pig farmer Andrew, 53, in North Yorkshire. Realizing life was short and it was time to make a decision, she sold her beloved salon in August 2011 and relocated to the farm in March 2012. Catherine is happy leading an incredibly down-to-earth life, rising at 6:30 am and working hard on the pig farm ever since. "For Lottery, my advice is just be sensible," she says. "Don't go crazy. Appreciate that happiness can't be bought."
According to a report from the University of California, the scores of the SAT and ACT college entrance tests can predict freshman success at UC campuses better than students' high school grades do.

The university has been under heavy pressure to drop the tests as an admission requirement, as some other colleges have done across the country. Board of Regents Chairman John A. Pérez, a powerful voice on the board, has been an opponent of the tests, who points out that scores are closely linked with families' education and that people with money can pay for tutoring to improve their children's scores.

But throwing out the tests entirely would be a mistake. A faculty review team took a year to examine the role of the admissions tests from every angle. And though it concluded that UC needed to do more to create equity (公平) in the way it evaluates student applications, its recommendation is to keep the tests.

The scores already are not counted as heavily as grades for admission, even though they are better predictors of success. And they can act as an important check against high schools that inflate (膨胀) student grades, as the report noted. That actually helps disadvantaged students more than wealthy ones because there is evidence that well-off schools are more likely to engage in grade inflation, the report said.

That's not to say the topic is settled and done. The report recommends eventually replacing SAT/ACT with a more UC-specific assessment. That might cause its own problems. Would applicants then have to deal with yet another test among the many required on the path to college?

A study called "Energy Awareness" conducted by the company Utility asked 2,000 UK homeowners what steps they had taken to ensure that their homes were energy efficient. The results show that just 25% UK homeowners have plans to make their houses more energy efficient. The study also revealed that the average Briton would only spend around £1,996 to make their homes more eco-friendly.

As for the question who is responsible for the current disappointing situation, respondents put the duty on the UK as a whole, saying residents should all be responsible. Meanwhile, large corporations should be next in line, followed by the government. But only 20% UK homeowners think the UK government has done enough to educate households about the importance of reducing their energy consumption.

Bill Richard, CEO of Utility, said, "To learn that 65% of UK homes aren't energy efficient comes with no surprise to me. Older houses are hard to mend and new builds are still not using the most effective materials."

The study also found just 55% have installed energy efficient lightbulbs (灯泡) at home in an effort to be more green. 50% of those polled, have chosen new wall materials, and 25% have started a compost pile (堆肥) for food waste.

Utility recently launched the "Energy High 5" movement, a positive energy-saving effort. It aims to welcome every UK household to learn about energy saving information and participate in fun activities and competitions that could help every household save up to £163 per year.

Bill said, "The greenest and cheapest energy is the energy we don't use. Let's make homes more efficient rather than generating more and more energy, which is just going to be wasted in the same way."

English language proficiency is critical to your success at UCLA. If all of your high school education was completed in English, you are considered proficient and do not need to satisfy this requirement. However, if you've completed all or some high school in a country where English was not the language of instruction, you will be required to demonstrate English proficiency if you have had less than 3 years of instruction in English.

To demonstrate English language proficiency, students are required to take the Test of English as a Foreign Language (TOEFL), the International English Language Testing Service (IELTS), or the Duolingo English Test (DET). We look for a competitive score above 100 (with sub-scores above 22) on the TOEFL, 7 or above on the IELTS, or a 120 or higher on the DET.

TOEFL, IELTS, and DET scores can be updated post-submission directly through the UC Application website. Note that while official test scores are not required to be sent along with the application for our review process, all test information must be accurately self-reported on the application site no later than January. You may send your TOEFL scores to one UC campus, and all campuses you apply to will receive them. However, IELTS and DET results must be sent to each campus you apply to. DET scores must be submitted through the DET testing portal (门户网站). Be sure to include your UC Application ID when sending DET scores.

If you're admitted to UCLA and your native language is not English, we may also require you to take UCLA's English-as-a-Second-Language Placement Examination (ESLPE) immediately before the term in which you enter.
Bicycles can be a great way for travelers to enjoy a city. Not only do you have easy access to many tourist spots, but they're good for your personal health, financial health and the planet's health.
However, not all cities are bicycle friendly. The good news is some cities have given bicycles and the practice of sustainability (可持续性) their due.

Bern, Switzerland
It's a great idea to see this nation's lovely capital by bike. There are routes to fit any fitness level or sightseeing interest.

The City of Bern route takes you through neighborhoods such as Kirchenfeld (the museum district). The UNESCO Tour route starts in Bern's Old Town and leads to the Rose Garden, a popular spot with a breathtaking view. It also goes by the Bern Cathedral and the city's mountain, the Gurten, before heading out to more rural settings. It's 60 kilometers with "easy" riding conditions.

Copenhagen, Denmark
The Danes (丹麦人) are known for taking their bicycling culture seriously. The first bike lane in Denmark was set up in 1892 in Copenhagen. Today, the capital has 385 kilometers of bike lanes. Bicyclists and drivers also safely share the same roadway in many places. Thanks to Danish design innovations (创新) such as narrowed streets and textured surfaces, cars drive slower.

For folks who love design, there's a 22-kilometer route that covers the buildings of innovative designer Bjarke Ingels. The Harbour Circle route offers 13 kilometers of waterside sites. Famous Tivoli Gardens is an easy ride from the center of the city, but you'll have to leave the bike outside the park. A bonus for tourists not in good shape: Copenhagen is mostly flat.
Researchers monitored 100 children ages 8 to 12 living in New Zealand. They found that the kids regularly slept between 8 and 11 hours a night and were considered generally healthy.
After one week of receiving 39 minutes less of sleep per night, the children reported lower overall well-being and ability to cope at school.

"We all know that we feel better with a good night's sleep, but there are very few data using experimental designs that actually show just how big the impact might be," said lead study author Rachael Taylor. "This sort of data is the only way we can 'prove' that changing one behavior actually does affect another."

The study covered many aspects of well-being, including an assessment of how the children felt physically, and psychologically, in their relationships with parents and friends, and how they felt about school.

Not all children were able to cut back their sleep up to a full hour in the study, but whatever amount they reduced caused a decline in their well-being. And the impacts were greater if the participants lost half an hour or more of sleep.

The children were monitored from July 4 to September 1, 2022, and there are still questions regarding the longer-term impacts. "We don't know what the long-term effect might be — maybe children adapt, maybe they don't and their well-being worsens even more," Taylor said. In the meantime, she advised families "not to underestimate the value of sleep and to prioritize sleep as much as is feasible."
It may be easy to brush off a little lost sleep, but getting less good-quality sleep could result in eating more food, worsening school performance and declines in mental health, Taylor added.
ChatGPT, the new artificial intelligence (AI) tool, is in use for only a few months, but it is already raising questions about the future of AI in education.

With many school systems in the U.S. still deciding how to set policies on the use of AI programs, New York City school officials recently started blocking the writing tool on school devices and networks.
ChatGPT was launched by OpenAI, a San Francisco-based company. But unlike previous AI tools, ChatGPT is available for free use on the Internet. It is also designed to be more user-friendly.
Millions of people have tried the tool. They used it to write poems or songs. Some tried to trick it into making mistakes. All of these are making it smarter.

The New York City education department said it is restricting the use of ChatGPT due to worries about its impacts on student learning, as well as "concerns regarding the safety and accuracy of content."

Jenna Lyle, a spokesperson for New York schools, said that the tool may provide quick and easy answers to questions, but "it does not build critical-thinking and problem-solving skills, which are essential for academic and lifelong success."

There is, however, no stopping students from using ChatGPT from home or on personal devices. Teachers are now trying to find out how to prevent students using the AI tool for cheating. In an open statement, OpenAI says that it plans to work with educators.

"We don't want ChatGPT to be used for misleading purposes in schools or anywhere else, so we're already developing mitigations (缓解办法) to help anyone identify texts generated by that system," the company said.

All the water on Earth has been here since the beginning. It cycles endlessly through the water cycle: from liquid rain to vapor (水蒸汽) in the air, to solid ice and snow. The water in our homes may have been frozen in a large mass of ice, flowed in the Amazon River, or even drunk by an elephant!

In nature, water is cleaned when it is filtered through soil or plants. Or, when water evaporates, all the pollutants are left behind and pure water molecules (分子) go to the air. People have created another method to recycle water. This process copies nature to clean water quickly so it can be reused again.

If you live in a town, all the used water in your home probably flows to a wastewater treatment plant, where the water is cleaned and then discharged. A typical recycled water treatment plant does not clean the water enough for drinking, but with a few extra steps the water can become drinkable again.

In Orange County, California, wastewater undergoes this extra treatment. After standard cleaning, water travels through microfiltration. Imagine a straw with very tiny holes, 300 times smaller than the width of a human hair. Water is pulled through these holes, leaving pollutants out. Next, this highly cleaned water goes through a system, which only allows pure water molecules to pass through. Even though this water is clean enough to drink, in Orange County it goes through one more final step. It's pumped (泵) deep into the ground where it mixes with groundwater and then is pumped back out and sent to the drinking water treatment plant before returning to people's homes.
Every year, The University of Cambridge awards over £100m in scholarships to new postgraduate students. The major internal sources of funding are:

The Cambridge Trust has been offering scholarships at Cambridge for over 30 years. In this time, it has awarded more than 20,000 scholarships to students from around the world.
The Trust awards around 500 scholarships a year to support the most outstanding students. It awards students at both PhD and Master's level, in all subjects, at any of the 31 Colleges.

Gates Cambridge Trust

The programme takes Masters and PhD students from any country outside the UK.

Harding Distinguished Postgraduate Scholarships
The Harding Distinguished Postgraduate Scholarship Programme was established in February 2019 thanks to an extraordinarily generous donation from the David and Claudia Harding Foundation. This is the biggest single gift made to a university in the UK by a British donor.
The programme awards at least 25 full scholarships each year to the most talented PhD students. Awardees can be from any nationality, studying any subject.

Mastercard Foundation Scholarship Programme
The Mastercard Foundation Scholarship Programme at Cambridge is designed to provide bright students from under-represented communities in Africa with fully-funded opportunities to complete their Master's training, develop leadership skills and contribute to sustainable (可持续的) futures in Africa.
The programme covers the cost of travel and visas, accommodation, meals, allowance for a personal computer, and a living stipend (津贴) — as well as tuition costs.

Multiple studies show that Gen Z, people from the ages of 16 to 26, prefer in-person shopping as much as online shopping, and more customers from that age group prefer physical stores than any other generation.

A report by the International Council of Shopping Centers (ICSC) shows 97 percent of respondents said they shop at brick-and-mortar stores and 95 percent said they shop online. "While members of Gen Z are digitally native consumers, they interact dynamically with brands both in-store and online," the study said.

Nicole Tan, 23, views items online but prefers making purchases in physical stores. "I like to try things on. If I see ads on social media and there are sales online, I'd maybe buy stuff online, but I usually like to shop in-store," she said.
The 23-year-old who works at a talent agency sometimes goes to the mall not to shop but to have dinner and go for a walk. "I do more leisure non-shopping things at the mall," she said.
Nicole is among others in her generation who visit shopping malls not only to shop but also to gather with friends.

Shopping malls in America have been struggling, particularly due to the growth of e-commerce in recent years and pandemic (流行病) restrictions. Stores are adapting to a new environment and targeting the Gen Z market, who might be leading the charge in reviving (复苏) in-person shopping experience.
They see malls as spaces to hang out and spend quality time with friends and family and would rather spend money on experiences than on material products, according to the ICSC.

To attract the young shoppers, malls are offering high-end dining and various activities and events. Thanks to those efforts and the increase of Gen Z shoppers, the dying America malls may soon welcome a promising revival.

Beavers (河狸), like humans, shape their ecosystems not just by eating or excreting (排泄), but also by building and tearing down. And because of those similarities, the rodents have become North America's best-known "ecosystem engineers."

But the scientific idea of ecosystem engineering wasn't born in a beaver "house" — it came from Negev Desert. Rock-eating snails (蜗牛) have a peculiar means of accessing food inside stones. They then excrete so much of the rock that they literally build the desert soil. When Clive Jones visited the desert in 1987, he saw that snails weren't the only animals shaping the landscape. Most of its organisms (生物) changed how water flowed in the dry environment. Jones and his colleagues created the term "ecosystem engineering" in 1994 to connect the processes they saw in that desert to similar ones all over the world.

Since the idea entered the scientific mainstream, ecologists have debated what counts as an engineer. Does an action have to be intentional, as beavers' dam-building appears to be? Does it need to shape the lives of other organisms?

Jones says no to both. In the view of an ecologist, it doesn't matter whether an elephant means to eat a specific plant — the fact is that it does. And the effect doesn't need to be significant. An animal's shadow is the least noticeable example of engineering. "No other organism cares about the shadow caused by the cat walking outside my window," Jones says. But the shadow has the same type of effect as a beaver's dam in that they both change the heat, light, water, and air that other organisms depend on.

Understanding how organisms alter landscapes isn't just an intellectual exercise — it's critical for figuring out how to preserve their fast-disappearing homes. "Human can imitate the way in which ecosystem engineers do their work," Jones says.

Overwhelming (令人不知所措的) and intense: that's how primary school teacher James Coleman describes the experience of his first two placements (实习课) in East London. "For the first 18 months I was like a rabbit in the headlights, and there were so many elements to absorb."

Soon, however, James realized it was time to challenge himself again. "I went on a couple of professional development courses at the Institute of Education (IOE), through which I met other Primary school teachers working in my area. We called our exchanges 'magpieing' — stealing each other's best ideas."

And he says the support he received from the IOE was invaluable. "I was enormously well-supported by the IOE, who set the highest standards and encouraged discussion. I was surrounded by high quality practitioners I could learn from. There were also 30 other passionate young teachers from my course at the IOE, and we were encouraged to network."

James is certain that without those connections he might not have made it through the course. "I remember feeling overwhelmed at times, but the support of like-minded people going through the same training was crucial. We would meet informally every Friday to discuss our week. It was education, education, education — we never talked about anything else!"

In his current role as Head of Operations and Training at the National Association of School-Based Teacher Trainers, one of James' priorities is to connect trainee teachers both to each other and to subject experts. "I am passionate that networking should be included in teaching practice."

James is also responsible for establishing mentoring (辅导) programs. "Mentoring is a formal process, with clear expectations, weekly reports and regular monitoring. Networking by contrast is far more informal and natural. It is important to remember that networks are not given to you: you have to join them in the first place."

The show "Emily in Paris" tells the story of a young Midwesterner struggling to adapt to a new culture after a promotion sends her to France. She gets the job despite not speaking French, which is highly unlikely in real life.

The story might have been more believable to me if the character were multilingual (多语的). Speaking and writing a second language are skills that U.S. Education Secretary Miguel Cardona frequently mentions as a superpower. He believes that these skills can lead to success in an increasingly global workforce. Encouraging students to become multilingual is one of his six focus areas, and he is pushing an initiative to transform the U.S. education system.

Such a national focus on promoting bilingualism is unusual. But it would mean finally encouraging millions of students whose first language is not English to retain their fluency while learning English. It would also emphasize the idea that native English speakers can expand career opportunities by learning a second language.

Cardona's tone is strikingly different from that of educational leaders in the recent past. For decades, students whose first language isn't English have been viewed as a liability, and were discouraged from using any language but English in the classroom.

Undoubtedly, the biggest difficulty in helping more students achieve proficiency in a second language is the lack of bilingual teachers, who are considered foreign language instructors and typically must earn bilingual certification.

The U.S. is one of the few countries considered monolingual, in comparison with most European countries where students begin learning a second language by the age of 9, according to the Pew Research Center. In 2017, the U.S. Department of Defense sponsored the National K-12 Foreign Language Enrollment Survey to determine the state of foreign language instruction in K-12 public schools. It found that only 11 states required foreign language study to graduate.

When the library in Northbridge announced that it would lend tools as well as books, some residents wondered whether it was moving away from its purpose. A library, they argued, should spend its limited budget on reading materials. The librarians agreed that books remained essential, but they also believed that a public library should give people access to useful resources they could not easily obtain on their own.

The idea came from a survey. Many residents said that they had small repair jobs at home but could not justify buying equipment they might use only once a year. Others lived in small apartments with nowhere to store it. The library therefore began with twenty basic tools donated by local businesses. Borrowers had to attend a short safety session, and electrical equipment was checked after every return. The service was free, although users paid for any damage caused by careless handling.

During the first six months, more than half of the borrowers had never held a library card before. Several stayed to explore the shelves after returning a tool. This did not prove that the service had increased reading across the town, as one newspaper claimed, but it did suggest that a different kind of resource could introduce new visitors to the building.

There were difficulties. Staff needed training, and checking equipment took longer than checking books. Rather than expand immediately, the library limited the number of loans each day and invited residents to give feedback. For the librarians, the question was not whether tools were better than books. It was how to offer the new service without weakening the services that people already depended on.

A software company recently allowed a group of employees to choose between a quiet room and a shared working area. The managers expected almost everyone to prefer silence. To their surprise, the employees did not make the same choice every day. Some entered the quiet room in the morning and returned to the shared area after lunch, while others did the opposite.

Interviews helped explain the pattern. Employees who were checking figures or writing detailed reports said that nearby conversations made it difficult to keep information in mind. Those discussing an early design often found the shared area helpful. Hearing a colleague ask an unexpected question could lead them to reconsider an assumption. The difference appeared to depend more on the task than on whether a person described themselves as quiet or sociable.

The company then introduced a simple booking system for the quiet room. It also set aside two hours each afternoon when conversations in the main office had to be kept low. This arrangement was not perfect. Some workers still used headphones, and a few preferred to complete demanding tasks at home. However, fewer people reported being interrupted at moments when they needed to concentrate.

The managers were careful about interpreting the results. The employees had volunteered for the trial, and the company had not measured whether their work became more accurate. A reduction in complaints was useful information, but it was not the same as proof of higher productivity. The company plans to compare several kinds of tasks over a longer period before changing the rest of its offices. Its experience suggests that a good workplace may need different spaces for different activities, rather than one arrangement that is supposed to suit everyone.

For years, residents of Westfield had asked for a direct bus to the regional hospital. The existing journey required a change in the city centre and often took more than an hour. When the council finally tested a direct route, however, the first month's passenger numbers were low. Some officials argued that the result showed there was little real demand and recommended ending the service.

Before making a decision, the transport team spoke to patients and hospital staff. They discovered that the bus arrived at the hospital at 9:40, while many morning appointments started before 9:30. The last return bus also left before afternoon appointments had finished. The route passed the right places, but its timetable did not match the reason many passengers needed to travel.

For the remaining two months of the trial, the team moved the first departure earlier and added a later return journey. They placed printed timetables in local pharmacies because some older residents rarely checked the council website. Passenger numbers gradually rose. A few people who had previously depended on relatives for a lift began travelling independently. Even so, the service still required public support to cover its costs.

At the final meeting, the council considered both the cost and the wider value of the route. It decided to continue the bus three days a week, choosing the days with the greatest demand. The transport team would review the arrangement after six months. The trial had not demonstrated that every requested bus route should run daily. It had shown that low use could reflect an unsuitable timetable or poor information, and that listening to potential passengers was necessary before judging whether a service was worth keeping.

On the first Saturday of each month, the hall behind a local cafe becomes a repair workshop. People arrive with lamps, radios and other small objects that no longer work. Volunteer repairers examine them while their owners watch. The owners pay for any replacement parts, but the volunteers do not charge for their time.

The workshop began when a retired engineer noticed how many electrical products were being thrown away because of simple faults. He did not promise that everything could be repaired. In fact, a damaged battery or an unavailable part sometimes makes repair impossible. The aim is to help people make an informed decision before buying a replacement.

At first, some visitors left their objects on a table and expected to collect them later. The organizers changed the booking notice to explain that owners must stay. Watching a repair often teaches them how the object works and how to care for it. A woman who had brought in a broken lamp later returned as a volunteer, helping visitors record faults before the repairers began.

After a year, the workshop had examined nearly three hundred items and repaired about half. The organizers also counted the conversations and skills shared as achievements. They plan to add a second session, but only when enough trained volunteers are available. A longer queue, they say, is a reason to recruit carefully, not a reason to promise more than the workshop can safely provide.

Shop owners on Green Street used to receive deliveries after nine in the morning. By then, customers were arriving and buses were filling the narrow road. Delivery vehicles often stopped outside shops for fifteen or twenty minutes, forcing cyclists into the middle of the traffic.

The town offered businesses a six-week trial of deliveries before seven. Several owners objected because someone would have to arrive early to receive goods. Residents living above the shops were also worried about noise. In response, the delivery company agreed to use small vehicles and move boxes on rubber-wheeled carts. Drivers received instructions not to leave engines running while unloading.

During the trial, journeys took less time because the roads were quieter. However, one bakery still needed a later delivery of fresh products. The town allowed it to keep its usual time rather than require every business to follow the same schedule. Two shops shared the cost of an early-morning assistant, who checked their goods and locked them in separate storage areas.

At the end of six weeks, most participating businesses wanted the arrangement to continue. Noise complaints had fallen after the first week, when drivers adjusted their unloading methods. The town plans to extend the trial to another street, while keeping a telephone number for residents to report problems. Earlier deliveries have eased traffic, but their success depends on organizing the work around both business needs and the people who live nearby.

篇章.标题: 并不显眼的博物馆标签
段落: When the Riverside Museum replaced its display labels, the change was easy to overlook. The objects stayed in the same cases, and the labels were still white with black text. Yet visitors began spending longer in one gallery and asking fewer questions about where objects had come from.

The old labels had been written mainly for specialists. They contained dates, technical names and descriptions of materials, but often failed to explain why an object mattered. A cooking pot, for instance, was described by its size and age without any mention of the family meals for which it had been used.

The new labels start with a short sentence about the object's role in everyday life. More detailed information follows underneath. Visitors who want an introduction can read the opening sentence, while those with a deeper interest can continue. The museum also tested several versions with people who rarely visit museums. Their questions helped staff identify unfamiliar words.

Not everyone welcomed the change. A few regular visitors worried that simpler language would mean less serious content. The museum answered by keeping full research notes available at the information desk. It had changed the order in which information was offered, not removed the evidence behind it. The experience showed that making an explanation easier to enter does not necessarily make it less accurate. Sometimes a familiar starting point allows readers to reach information they would otherwise have passed by.

At Eastgate College, students used to advertise unwanted textbooks on separate social media pages. Buyers sometimes travelled across campus only to discover that a book was an older edition than the one required. Sellers, meanwhile, received the same questions repeatedly and found it difficult to arrange meetings.

The student union created a shared list containing the title, edition, condition and asking price of each book. It did not set prices or collect payments. Its role was to make information easier to compare. Sellers uploaded a photograph of the page showing the edition number, and buyers were advised to check their reading lists before making contact.

A market held during the first week of term added another benefit. Students could inspect books and meet sellers in a public place. Unsold books could be collected by a local charity, but donation was optional. The union made this clear after several students assumed that leaving a book on a table meant it would automatically be donated.

The market helped many students save money, though it did not solve every problem. Some courses used new editions that were unavailable second-hand. The union therefore asked departments to publish reading lists earlier and to explain when an older edition would be acceptable. Better information from teachers, it discovered, could matter as much as a better place to buy and sell.

A restaurant introduced a small charge for bottled water while continuing to offer tap water free. The owner expected most customers to welcome the choice. Instead, several online reviews complained that water had become expensive. The menu placed the two options on different pages, and customers who saw the bottled-water price did not always notice the free alternative.

The owner first considered reducing the price. A waiter suggested a simpler experiment: list both choices together and ask every table which one it preferred. Staff would also explain that the tap water was filtered on the premises. The wording was kept factual, without suggesting that customers who chose bottles were making a poor decision.

Over the following month, requests for free tap water increased and complaints about the price almost disappeared. Bottled-water sales fell, but the restaurant also spent less time responding to unhappy customers. The owner could not tell whether overall spending had changed, because a new lunch menu had been introduced during the same period.

The experience led her to review other parts of the menu. She found that a clear choice could be more useful than a lower price that customers did not understand. A business may technically offer an option, she concluded, yet customers cannot benefit from it unless they can see it at the moment they need to decide.

After heavy rain, water used to collect beside the entrance to Hillview School. The usual solution would have been a larger drain. Instead, a landscape designer proposed a shallow garden that could temporarily hold rainwater and allow it to sink slowly into the soil.

The school chose a patch of unused ground away from the main path. Plants that could tolerate both wet and dry conditions were added. The garden was not intended to remain full of water; under normal conditions, collected rain would disappear within a day. A small overflow pipe carried extra water away during particularly strong storms.

Students helped measure rainfall and photographed the garden each week. They soon noticed that the surface could look dry while the soil below still held moisture. This became a practical lesson in how water moves through the ground. Maintenance staff also learned to remove rubbish from the inlet, since even a well-designed garden would work poorly if water could not enter it.

The first year brought fewer puddles near the entrance, although the school had not experienced an exceptionally severe storm. Staff therefore avoided claiming that flooding had been eliminated. The garden was one part of a wider drainage system. It offered a useful combination of water management and teaching, provided that its limits were understood and routine care continued.

社区图书馆 are changing the way people use shared spaces. In one town, a small project began with a simple idea: make useful resources easier for everyone to reach. The first volunteers collected information, repaired equipment, and asked residents what they needed most.

The project now offers reading rooms and digital resources. It also keeps a clear schedule so that visitors know when activities are available. Because the service is free or inexpensive, students, older people, and busy workers can all benefit from it.

Organizers say the most valuable result is not a single building or machine. It is the habit of cooperation. Residents contribute time, share suggestions, and learn from one another. These actions make the project more accessible and help it continue.

The experience shows that practical improvements do not always require a large budget. When a community identifies a real need and works patiently, a modest plan can create lasting changes in everyday life.
